text:
If you’ve ever sorted your recycling, you’ve probably wondered how much of it is actually worth something. My research team at StoneComms has been looking at what that question means for African cities.

There’s a rather important distinction between the value of what’s in a rubbish bag and the cost of collecting the bag in the first place.

In Kampala, the city has expanded its network of licensed collectors. In South Africa, a packaging recovery scheme funded by producers takes account of the cost of collecting, sorting and transporting materials, as well as the money earned from selling them. The two examples are quite different, but they help explain why a market for recycled plastic doesn't necessarily pay for a dependable rubbish collection service.

The team suggests keeping two sets of accounts: one for the cost of providing the public service, and another for the money that can realistically be made from recovering materials. Where the second helps pay for the first, make that contribution clear. But don't rely on an optimistic recycling forecast to fund next month's collection rounds.

There's a human side to this, too. Many people already earn a living collecting and sorting discarded materials. A new municipal contract might look more efficient on paper while taking away their access to the very materials they depend on. I'd want to know what happens to those livelihoods, and how households that struggle to pay will still get their rubbish collected.

Here's the paper, if you're interested:
https://stonecomms.com/research/municipal-waste-finance-africa-collection-recycling-public-service

Tomorrow the team will be sharing another piece, this time on African vaccine manufacturing. It asks what happens between being invited to supply vaccines and receiving an actual order that a factory can plan around. It's a different industry, but again, knowing who will pay, and when, matters enormously.

Both papers are free to read. You can follow the research team here:
https://www.linkedin.com/company/stonecomms/

And if you're working on an African infrastructure or investment question that deserves a closer look, do get in touch. I'd be interested to hear about it.
